svg.title: Failure convergence on the same visual scale: VPLS pays three stages and about forty five seconds, EVPN one withdraw and about three
svg.desc: Two timelines drawn to the same scale. On the VPLS timeline three blocks follow a failure: detection at three seconds, MAC ageing at thirty seconds and re-flooding with re-learning at twelve, totalling about forty five seconds. On the EVPN timeline a single short block covers BFD detection, one BGP withdraw and a FIB update, about three seconds, drawn roughly a fifteenth of the length. A bracket between them marks the forty two seconds of downtime the design either pays or avoids. A box on the right explains why EVPN is fast: an Ethernet auto-discovery route withdraws a whole ESI in one update, MAC routes are pre-installed so nothing is flooded, and the designated forwarder was elected before the failure.
svg.text: Same failure, same scale: what VPLS spends its time on is not the failure, it is the forgetting
Both bars start at the same instant. The length of the second bar is the argument for a control plane
EVPN · BFD, one withdraw, FIB update
42 seconds of downtime the design either pays or does not
installed, so nothing has to be
BUM forwarding has no vote to hold.
none of this needs faster hardware
The 30-second block is the one that matters. Detection is engineering; ageing is a timer inherited from a learning bridge that had no other option in 1990.
EVPN keeps the timer where it belongs — in the control plane, where a withdrawal can be reasoned about, filtered and measured.
Design consequence: the smaller number is not only faster, it is provable. You can state the convergence budget in the design document and test it with a link pull.
